Cash Conversion Cycle

The CCC measures how quickly you turn investments in inventory and operations into cash from sales. Every day you reduce it is cash back in your hands.

Formula
CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO
How to improve it
Negotiate shorter payment terms with customers to reduce DSO
Extend supplier payment terms to increase DPO
Reduce safety stock and improve demand forecasting to shrink DIO
Offer early payment discounts to accelerate receivables

Inflation & Pricing

When input costs rise, how much do you need to raise prices to protect gross profit? Higher gross margin means less price increase required — the GM lever shows this directly.

Breakeven price increase
Price increase needed = (1 − GM%) × inflation rate
40% GM, 8% inflation → 4.8% price increase needed
60% GM, 8% inflation → 3.2% price increase needed
Higher GM = less price increase required
Pricing strategies
Improving GM before an inflationary period reduces how much price increase you need
Tier price increases by customer segment — protect key accounts, raise on transactional
Use value-based framing, not cost-plus language, when announcing increases
Lock in supplier costs with longer contracts before raising customer prices

Revenue Mix Shift

Where your revenue comes from matters as much as how much of it you make. Shifting toward higher-margin product lines improves blended profitability without growing top-line revenue.

Blended margin formula
Blended margin = Σ (segment % × segment margin)
How to shift the mix
Incentivize sales reps on margin contribution, not just revenue
Bundle low-margin hardware with high-margin SaaS to shift perceived value
Raise prices on hardware; use software as the growth engine
Track customer lifetime value by product segment, not just ARR

Breakeven Analysis

Every fixed cost increase requires extra revenue to break even. The higher your gross margin, the less extra revenue you need. This is the single most important relationship in business cost decisions.

The formula
Extra revenue needed = Fixed cost increase ÷ GM%
$100K cost at 40% GM → $250K extra revenue needed
$100K cost at 20% GM → $500K extra revenue needed
$100K cost at 60% GM → $167K extra revenue needed
Before approving any fixed cost
Ask: is the incremental revenue it generates greater than FC increase ÷ GM%?
Every 1 point of GM improvement reduces the revenue required per dollar of fixed cost
Convert fixed costs to variable where possible — reduces risk when revenue is uncertain
A new hire, lease, or subscription all follow this same formula — run the number first

Customer Retention

Churn compounds in both directions. A small improvement in retention rate is worth far more than it appears in year one — because those customers stay to generate revenue in years two and three as well.

Retained customers (year n)
Customers × (1 − churn rate)ⁿ
Retention levers
Identify at-risk accounts 60–90 days before renewal using health scores
Invest in onboarding — most churn is decided in the first 90 days
Annual contracts reduce churn by ~3–5 points vs. monthly billing
Run win-back campaigns within 30 days of cancellation — highest conversion window

Price Increase Impact

When you raise prices, your margin per unit improves — so you can afford to lose some volume and still deliver the same gross profit dollars. This shows exactly how much volume loss you can absorb.

Discount Impact

Discounts cut your margin per unit — so you need to sell more just to break even on gross profit dollars. This shows how much additional revenue you must generate to stay whole.

Price increase formula
Max volume drop % = price increase % ÷ (original margin % + price increase %)
Discount formula
Extra revenue needed = (discount % × original revenue) ÷ (original margin % − discount %)
Pricing guidance
A 10% price increase on a 40% margin business lets you lose 20% of volume and still break even on GM $
Most businesses overestimate how much volume they'll lose from a price increase
At higher margins, price increases become significantly more powerful — protect your margin first
Segment your customer base and test increases on lower-risk accounts first
Discount guidance
A 10% discount on a 40% margin business requires 33% more revenue to break even — that's rarely achievable
At thin margins, even small discounts require enormous volume increases to compensate
Offer non-price concessions (extended terms, extra support) instead of straight discounts
Track average selling price per rep — discount creep is often invisible until you look

Equipment Replacement ROI

Replacing broken or aging equipment adds depreciation as a new fixed cost — but saves on maintenance and recovers lost revenue from downtime. This model shows the net annual cost change and how much extra revenue you need to break even.

Core formulas
Annual depreciation = (Price − Salvage) ÷ Life
Net cost change = Depreciation − Maintenance savings
Downtime revenue = Hours × Revenue/hr × GM%
Extra revenue needed = Net cost change ÷ GM%
Decision framework
If downtime revenue recovered exceeds net cost change, the equipment is self-funding — no new sales needed
Payback under 3 years is generally strong; over 5 years warrants scrutiny at typical cost of capital
Get maintenance cost data from service records — estimates are usually too low
Include installation, training, and lost production during switchover in the purchase price
If the old equipment is broken, its downtime hours may be 100% of capacity — factor that in

Operating Leverage

Operating leverage measures how much a change in revenue amplifies into profit. High fixed costs mean high leverage — profits rise fast when revenue grows, but fall fast when it drops. A double-edged sword every small business owner needs to understand.

Core formulas
Operating leverage = Gross profit ÷ EBIT
EBIT = Gross profit − Fixed costs
% profit change = % revenue change × leverage
e.g. leverage of 4× means a 10% revenue rise → 40% profit rise, and a 10% revenue drop → 40% profit drop
Why this matters for small business
Every time you sign a lease, hire a salaried employee, or commit to a software contract, you increase your operating leverage. You are betting that revenue will grow enough to justify the fixed cost.

Before adding ANY fixed cost, ask: how much revenue do I need to cover this? Use the Breakeven tab — it answers exactly that question.
What this means for your business
High leverage is great in growth — but in a downturn it's the businesses with lower fixed costs that survive
Every new fixed cost (hire, lease, subscription) increases leverage and raises your breakeven
Improving gross margin reduces the leverage needed to be profitable — protect GM first
If leverage is above 5×, a 20% revenue drop could wipe out most or all of your profit
Convert fixed costs to variable where possible — commission vs salary, usage-based vs subscription

Before committing to any fixed cost — ask these 3 questions:
1
What is the breakeven revenue this creates?
Fixed Cost ÷ GM% — at 80% GM a $50K fixed cost needs — in extra revenue
2
How confident am I that revenue will exceed that breakeven?
Most cost overruns come from optimistic revenue assumptions — be honest.
3
Can I make this cost variable instead?
Contract vs hire · Month-to-month vs long lease · Pay-per-use vs subscription

FC vs VC: Six Key Effects

Your cost structure — fixed vs variable — shapes every aspect of your business: where profit begins, how sensitive it is to revenue swings, how resilient you are in downturns, how fast you scale, how you manage cash, and what decisions you're forced to make under pressure.

The two businesses modelled
High FC: FC=$300K · VC=20%
→ Gross margin = 80%
→ Breakeven = $375K

High VC: FC=$50K · VC=70%
→ Gross margin = 30%
→ Breakeven = $167K
Summary: the six effects
Breakeven: high FC needs more revenue before any profit; high VC starts profiting sooner
Volatility: high FC amplifies profit swings in both directions
Downside: high VC self-adjusts — costs fall with revenue, preserving survival
Scalability: high FC delivers explosive profit growth past breakeven
Cash flow: high FC demands reserves; high VC breathes with revenue
Decisions: every fixed cost is a bet — run Fixed Cost ÷ GM% first

DSCR & Debt Schedule

DSCR = EBITDA ÷ Total Debt Service. Debt service is the actual amortised principal + interest for each year — which changes every year as the balance reduces. EBITDA grows with revenue. This shows why a business with sub-0.8× DSCR today may still qualify for a loan if the trajectory is credible.

Expense Cuts to 1.25×

Each slider shows a specific expense category and a realistic action to reduce it. The goal is to show the lender exactly which costs come out and why — not just a top-down number.

DSCR formula
EBITDA = Gross profit − Operating expenses
Debt service = Principal + Interest (yr)
DSCR = EBITDA ÷ Debt service
<0.8× = serious problem
0.8–1.0× = can't cover debt
1.0–1.25× = lender danger zone
1.25×+ = lender minimum
1.5×+ = comfortable
Presenting this to a lender
Show the trajectory — a DSCR moving from 0.7× to 1.3× over 3 years tells a better story than a static snapshot
Be specific about each expense cut — "reduce payroll by $30K by not replacing one departing role" beats "cut overhead"
EBITDA adds back D&A — use it, not net income, to show true cash-generating ability
Extending the loan term reduces annual debt service and can push DSCR above threshold without any P&L change

Cash flow statement — indirect method

Profit is an Opinion. Cash is a Fact.

You can show profit on your income statement and still run out of cash. This model shows exactly why — working capital growth, capex, loan payments, and owner draws all consume cash that never appears as an expense.

Cash from operations
Net income
+ Depreciation (non-cash)
− Increase in A/R (cash out)
− Increase in inventory (cash out)
+ Increase in A/P (cash in)
= Cash from operations
The biggest cash traps
Rapid revenue growth forces A/R and inventory up — cash drains even as profit rises
Buying equipment is not an expense — it doesn't reduce profit but it does consume cash
Loan principal repayments are cash out but never hit the income statement
Owner draws are not an expense on the P&L — but they absolutely drain the bank account
Monitor cash from operations every month — if it's below net income, find out why

Your ratios vs RMA industry benchmarks

Ratio Dashboard

Ratios turn raw numbers into benchmarkable intelligence. Green = at or above industry standard. Amber = watch it. Red = action needed. Compare yours against RMA (Risk Management Association) benchmarks used by lenders.

Key ratios
Current = Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities
Quick = (Cash + A/R) ÷ Current Liabilities
Debt-to-Equity = Total Liabilities ÷ Equity
Gross Margin = Gross Profit ÷ Sales
Net Margin = Net Profit ÷ Sales
DSO = A/R ÷ (Sales ÷ 365)
DIO = Inventory ÷ (COGS ÷ 365)
DPO = A/P ÷ (COGS ÷ 365)
How lenders read ratios
Current ratio below 1.0 means you can't pay current bills — a red flag for any lender
Debt-to-equity above 3× signals the business is heavily leveraged and fragile
DSO trending up means customers are paying slower — a hidden cash drain
Gross margin declining year over year is the single most important warning signal

Where cash goes during growth

Growth Eats Cash

Fast-growing businesses are among the most likely to run out of cash — even while profitable. When revenue grows 30%, your A/R, inventory, and supplier payments all grow 30% too. The cash goes out before the revenue comes in.

Cash needed for growth
ΔA/R = revenue growth × (DSO ÷ 365)
ΔInventory = revenue growth × (DIO ÷ 365) × COGS%
ΔA/P = revenue growth × (DPO ÷ 365) × COGS%

Working capital needed = ΔA/R + ΔInventory − ΔA/P
Total cash needed = WC needed + Capex
Managing growth cash
Tighten DSO before growing — faster collections mean growth funds itself
Negotiate extended supplier terms (DPO) before ramping up revenue
A line of credit sized to fund working capital growth should be in place before you need it
Profitable but cash-negative growth is the #1 reason healthy businesses fail
Calculate your cash intensity before accepting a large contract — know what it costs to fund

Service Business KPIs

Service firms sell time and expertise. Utilization (how much capacity bills), gross margin, and client retention are the core levers. DSO directly determines how much cash is floating in unpaid invoices.

Key relationships
Effective rate = Revenue ÷ Billable hrs
A/R tied up = Revenue × (DSO ÷ 365)
Client LTV = Avg revenue ÷ (1 − Retention)
RMA / IBIS Benchmarks
Gross margin: 35–55%; 50%+ strong
Utilization: 65–75% healthy; below 60% red flag
Revenue/employee: $100–250K typical; $300K+ excellent
Net margin: 10–20% strong
Retention: 85%+ target; below 75% crisis
DSO: Under 45 days; over 60 = A/R risk
DPO: 20–30 days typical for service firms

Construction KPIs

Profit is made or lost in the field. Estimating accuracy, overhead discipline, and change order management separate 5% from 15% net margins. DSO is critical — getting paid before you must pay subs protects cash flow.

Key relationships
Net margin = Gross margin − Overhead %
A/R float = Revenue × (DSO ÷ 365)
Job variance = (Actual − Est) ÷ Est
Backlog burn = Revenue ÷ 12/month
AGC / RMA Benchmarks
Gross margin: 15–25% GC; 25–40% specialty
Overhead ratio: 8–15% of revenue
DSO: 45–60 days typical; under 45 strong
DPO: 30–45 days; pay subs after you collect
Backlog: 3–6 months healthy; under 2 = risk
Job cost variance: Under 3% excellent; 10%+ = problem
Change order win rate: 80%+ target
TRIR (safety): Under 2.0 below avg; under 1.0 excellent

Retail & Distribution KPIs

Profitability lives in the spread between gross margin and occupancy/labor, amplified by inventory velocity. DIO and DPO are your two biggest working capital levers — faster turns and longer payment terms free cash without borrowing.

Key relationships
DIO = 365 ÷ Inventory turns
CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO
WC tied up = Revenue × (CCC ÷ 365)
GMROI = Gross margin $ ÷ Avg inventory cost
NRF / RMA Benchmarks
Gross margin: 30–50% specialty; 20–30% distribution
Inventory turns: 4–8× specialty; 10–20× distribution
DIO: 46–91 days specialty; 18–37 days distribution
DSO: Near 0 retail; 15–30 days wholesale/B2B
DPO: 30–45 days; negotiate terms aggressively
Sales/sq ft: $200–400 typical; $500+ strong
Net margin: 2–6% retail; 1–4% distribution
Shrinkage: ~1.6% avg; under 1% excellent
Return rate: 5–10% in-store; 20–30% e-commerce
